question: Define criminal intimidation under Section 351 of the BNS and explain its graded punishments.
modelAnswer: Under s.351(1) (formerly s.503 IPC), whoever threatens another by any means with any injury to his person, reputation or property, or to the person or reputation of anyone in whom that person is interested, with intent to cause alarm to that person, or to cause him to do any act he is not legally bound to do, or to omit any act he is legally entitled to do, as the means of avoiding the execution of the threat, commits criminal intimidation. The Explanation extends it to threats to injure the reputation of a deceased person in whom the person threatened is interested, and the Illustration gives the example of threatening to burn B's house to make him give up a civil suit. The ingredients are: (1) a threat, by any means (words, letters, phone calls, electronic messages); (2) of injury to person, reputation or property of the victim or someone he is interested in; and (3) intent to cause alarm, or to compel an act or omission against the victim's legal position. The threat need not be carried out, and the offender need not have the means to carry it out, provided the intent is present. Punishments: (2) up to two years, or fine, or both; (3) if the threat is to cause death or grievous hurt, destruction of property by fire, an offence punishable with death, life or seven years or more, or to impute unchastity to a woman — up to seven years, or fine, or both; (4) if made by anonymous communication or with precautions to conceal the threatener's name or abode — up to two years in addition to the punishment for the offence. The offence is non-cognizable and bailable; sub-ss. (2) and (3) are compoundable by the person intimidated. The BNS merges ss.503, 506 and 507 IPC and adds 'by any means' to the definition.

question: Define defamation under Section 356. Explain the Explanations that widen or limit its scope.
modelAnswer: Under s.356(1) (formerly s.499 IPC), whoever, by words spoken or intended to be read, by signs, or by visible representations, makes or publishes in any manner any imputation concerning a person, intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that it will harm, his reputation, is said to defame that person, except in the excepted cases. The ingredients are: (1) making or publishing an imputation; (2) concerning a person; (3) by words, signs or visible representations; (4) with intent, knowledge or reason to believe that it will harm reputation; and (5) not falling within any Exception. Publication — communication to someone other than the person defamed — is essential. The Explanations shape its scope. Explanation 1: an imputation about a deceased person may be defamation if it would harm his reputation if living and is intended to hurt his family or near relatives. Explanation 2: a company, association or collection of persons as such can be defamed. Explanation 3: an imputation in the form of an alternative or expressed ironically can be defamation — the Illustrations show insinuation ('Z is an honest man; he never stole B's watch'), pointing at someone, and a drawing all count. Explanation 4 limits the offence: an imputation harms reputation only if, directly or indirectly, in the estimation of others, it lowers the person's moral or intellectual character, lowers his character in respect of his caste or calling, lowers his credit, or causes it to be believed that his body is in a loathsome or disgraceful state. Defamation is punishable under s.356(2) with simple imprisonment up to two years, or fine, or both, or community service; it is non-cognizable, bailable and compoundable by the person defamed.

question: Discuss the Exceptions to defamation under Section 356.
modelAnswer: Section 356 contains ten Exceptions. (1) Truth for the public good: it is not defamation to impute anything true about a person if it is for the public good that it be made or published — truth alone is not enough; public good is also required, and it is a question of fact. (2) Public conduct of public servants: good-faith opinion on a public servant's conduct in discharging public functions, and his character so far as it appears in that conduct. (3) Conduct on public questions: good-faith opinion on anyone's conduct touching a public question, and his character as it appears in that conduct — for example his conduct in petitioning Government, attending public meetings or canvassing for a candidate. (4) Reports of court proceedings: publishing a substantially true report of court proceedings or their result; a Magistrate or officer holding a preliminary inquiry in open court counts as a court. (5) Merits of decided cases: good-faith opinion on the merits of a decided case, or on the conduct of a party, witness or agent in it, and on their character so far as it appears in that conduct. (6) Merits of public performances: good-faith opinion on a book, speech, acting, singing or other work submitted to public judgment, and on the author's character so far as it appears in that work. (7) Censure by a person in lawful authority: a judge, head of department, parent, teacher, master or banker censuring in good faith those under his lawful authority. (8) Accusation to authority: preferring in good faith an accusation to someone with lawful authority over the person, such as a complaint to a Magistrate, master or father. (9) Protection of interests: a good-faith imputation for the protection of one's own or another's interests or for the public good — such as a shopkeeper warning his manager not to give credit to a customer. (10) Caution: conveying a caution in good faith to one person against another for his good, or that of someone he is interested in, or for the public good. Except the first and fourth, all require good faith, and Exceptions 2, 3, 5 and 6 protect opinion only so far as the character appears in the relevant conduct, 'and no further'.

question: Explain Section 353 (statements conducing to public mischief). How has the BNS addressed fake news?
modelAnswer: Section 353 (formerly s.505 IPC) punishes whoever makes, publishes or circulates any statement, false information, rumour or report, including through electronic means: (1)(a) with intent, or likely, to cause any officer, soldier, sailor or airman of the Army, Navy or Air Force to mutiny or otherwise disregard or fail in his duty; (b) with intent, or likely, to cause fear or alarm to the public or a section of it whereby anyone may be induced to commit an offence against the State or against public tranquillity; or (c) with intent, or likely, to incite any class or community to commit an offence against another — up to three years, or fine, or both. Under s.353(2), making, publishing or circulating any statement or report containing false information, rumour or alarming news, including through electronic means, with intent or likely to create or promote enmity, hatred or ill-will between religious, racial, language or regional groups, castes or communities on any ground is punishable with up to three years, or fine, or both; under s.353(3), if done in a place of worship or religious assembly, up to five years and fine. The Exception protects a person who has reasonable grounds for believing the statement, information, rumour or report to be true and who makes or circulates it in good faith without the prohibited intent. Classification: s.353(1) is non-cognizable and non-bailable; s.353(2)-(3) are cognizable and non-bailable. The BNS addresses fake news by expressly adding 'false information' to the kinds of content covered and 'including through electronic means' to the modes of circulation, so that forwarding false messages on social media and messaging apps clearly falls within the section. Related provisions are s.196 (promoting enmity) and s.197(1)(d) (false or misleading information jeopardising India's sovereignty).

question: Distinguish between criminal intimidation (Section 351) and extortion (Section 308).
modelAnswer: Both involve putting a person in fear, but they differ in their object and completion. (1) Object: extortion requires that the victim be dishonestly induced to deliver property, a valuable security or a signed or sealed document; criminal intimidation requires only intent to cause alarm, or to make the victim do or omit any act against his legal position — property need not be involved at all. (2) Completion: extortion is complete only when property is delivered; criminal intimidation is complete as soon as the threat is made with the required intent. (3) Dishonesty: extortion requires dishonest inducement (wrongful gain or loss); criminal intimidation does not. (4) Threat: in both, the threat can be of injury to person, reputation or property of the victim or someone he is interested in. (5) Punishment and classification: extortion up to seven years (more in aggravated forms), cognizable; criminal intimidation up to two years (seven years for serious threats), non-cognizable and compoundable. A threat made to extract money that does not succeed may amount to criminal intimidation and to the offence under s.308(3) or (4) of putting in fear to commit extortion.

question: Problem: A, a local politician, tells a public meeting that B, the municipal commissioner, 'has taken bribes from every builder in town' and 'is a drunkard who beats his wife'. A has no proof of either claim. Discuss A's liability for defamation and any defences.
modelAnswer: A made imputations concerning B by spoken words at a public meeting, so there is publication. Both imputations — bribe-taking and drunkenness with domestic violence — would lower B's moral character in the estimation of others (Explanation 4), and A clearly knew or had reason to believe they would harm B's reputation. The ingredients of s.356(1) are satisfied, subject to the Exceptions. Exception 1 (truth for the public good) is not available, because A has no proof; he would have to prove that the imputations are true and that publishing them was for the public good. Exception 2 protects good-faith opinion on a public servant's conduct in the discharge of his public functions, and his character so far as it appears in that conduct. The bribery allegation relates to B's official conduct, but Exception 2 protects opinions, not assertions of fact made without any basis; making such a serious factual accusation without proof and without due care and attention (the test of good faith under s.2) is unlikely to be in good faith. The allegation that B is a drunkard who beats his wife does not relate to B's public functions at all, so Exception 2 cannot apply to it — the protection extends to his character only so far as it appears in his public conduct, 'and no further'. Exception 9 (protection of interests or public good) also requires good faith, which is lacking. A is therefore liable under s.356(2): simple imprisonment up to two years, or fine, or both, or community service. The offence is non-cognizable, bailable, triable by a Magistrate of the first class, and compoundable by B. B could also claim damages in a civil suit for defamation.

question: Explain Sections 354, 355 and 357 of the BNS.
modelAnswer: Section 354 (formerly s.508 IPC) punishes whoever voluntarily causes or attempts to cause a person to do what he is not legally bound to do, or to omit what he is legally entitled to do, by inducing or attempting to induce him to believe that he or someone in whom he is interested will be rendered an object of Divine displeasure by some act of the offender if he does not comply. The punishment is up to one year, or fine, or both; it is non-cognizable, bailable and compoundable by the person induced. The Illustrations mention sitting in dharna at Z's door to make it believed that Z will incur Divine displeasure, and threatening to kill one's own child in circumstances where the killing would be believed to bring Divine displeasure on Z. Section 355 (formerly s.510 IPC) punishes whoever, in a state of intoxication, appears in any public place, or any place which it is a trespass for him to enter, and there conducts himself so as to cause annoyance to any person — simple imprisonment up to twenty-four hours, or fine up to ₹1,000, or both, or community service; non-cognizable and bailable. Community service is new. Section 357 (formerly s.491 IPC) punishes whoever, being bound by a lawful contract to attend on or supply the wants of a person who, by reason of youth, unsoundness of mind, disease or bodily weakness, is helpless or incapable of providing for his own safety or wants, voluntarily omits to do so — up to three months, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both; non-cognizable, bailable and compoundable by the person with whom the offender contracted. It is the only surviving criminal breach-of-contract-of-service provision.

question: Problem: C sends D a WhatsApp message from an unknown number saying D's daughter will be 'disfigured with acid' unless D withdraws a police complaint against C's brother. Discuss C's liability.
modelAnswer: C threatened D, by an electronic message (covered by 'by any means'), with injury to the person of someone in whom D is interested — his daughter — intending to cause D to omit an act he is legally entitled to do, namely pursuing a police complaint. This is criminal intimidation under s.351(1). The threat is to cause grievous hurt (disfigurement by acid), so the aggravated punishment under s.351(3) applies: up to seven years, or fine, or both. C sent the message from an unknown number, taking precautions to conceal where the threat came from, so s.351(4) adds up to two years in addition to the punishment for the offence. C may also be liable under s.225 (threat of injury to induce a person to refrain from applying for protection to a public servant), since a police complaint is a legal application for protection, and under s.232 if the complaint has reached court and the threat is aimed at making D give false evidence. Criminal intimidation is non-cognizable and bailable; s.351(3) is triable by a Magistrate of the first class and compoundable by D, though s.351(4) is not listed for compounding.
